title: Dambun Rago
localName: Dambun rago — dambu nama, dried beef floss
author: Khadijat Lawal
desc: The ram version — boiled until it falls apart, shredded, respiced with yaji, garlic and ginger, and shallow-fried five to ten minutes a batch.
longDesc: This is dambu made with ram rather than beef, which by the northern naming system makes it properly dambun rago. The method is the same shape: boil the meat with spices until it is very tender and falling apart, shred it by continuous turning, pounding, or with a mallet or rolling pin, then add more spices — yaji, seasoning cubes, garlic and ginger — and shallow-fry in batches for five to ten minutes. No quantities are given for any ingredient, which is recorded rather than filled, and the texture target is the same: soft and chewy, neither greasy nor excessively crunchy.
ingredients: Chilli powder — see the note; it never appears in the method
equipment: Mortar and pestle, mallet, or rolling pin and chopping board
steps: Boil the ram meat with the spices — salt, seasoning cubes, ginger powder — and onions, till it is very tender and falls apart.
Shred the meat by continuous turning, by pounding, or with a mallet or rolling pin on a chopping board.
After shredding, add some more spices — yaji, seasoning cubes, garlic and ginger.
Heat the vegetable oil in a large pan and shallow-fry the shredded meat in batches, 5 to 10 minutes per batch.
Aim for soft and chewy, avoiding both greasiness and excessive crunchiness.
chefTips: Falls apart is the boiling cue here, which is further than the beef version's 'softens and the liquid evaporates'. Ram is tougher and needs it.
Soft and chewy, avoiding greasy and avoiding crunchy. That is the stated target and it is the same language the beef version uses — but without the temperature.
For the frying temperature use the beef version's figure, 165 to 170°C (NGA091). This page gives none, and the oil temperature is what decides the texture.
Spice twice: once in the boiling water, once after shredding. The second round is where most of the flavour lands.
Five to ten minutes per batch, and genuinely in batches. Crowding the pan drops the temperature and you get greasy floss.
No quantities are given on this page for anything. Use the beef version's 2 kg of meat to a tablespoon of yaji as a starting ratio.
By the northern naming system this is dambun rago rather than dambu nama — rago is ram, nama and saniya are beef.
commonMistakes: Stopping the boil before the meat falls apart.
Frying without controlling the oil temperature.
Adding all the spice in the boiling water.
Expecting it to shred when there is still liquid in the pot.
sources: Adapted from 'How to prepare dried beef floss (Dambu nama)', byline 'ByKhadijat Kuburat Lawal', Daily Trust. Cooking time in the article header: 30 to 40 minutes.

NO QUANTITIES ARE SPECIFIED FOR ANY INGREDIENT on this page. The list is reproduced bare, exactly as printed: Ram meat; Seasoning cubes and salt; Chilli powder; Onion; Garlic; Yaji (suya spice); Vegetable oil; Ginger powder. That is recorded as a finding; the starting ratio suggested in the tips is labelled as coming from the other recipe.

Method as printed: 'Boil the ram meat with the spices (salt, seasoning cubes, ginger powder) and onions till it is very tender i.e. it falls apart'; shred by continuous turning, pounding, or with a mallet or rolling pin on a chopping board; 'After shredding, add some more spices (yaji, seasoning cubes, garlic and ginger)'; heat vegetable oil in a large pan and shallow-fry in batches 5 to 10 minutes per batch.

DONENESS CUE as printed: the oil temperature must produce 'soft and chewy' results, avoiding both greasiness and excessive crunchiness — the same language the Kitchen Butterfly version uses, but WITHOUT the temperature figure. The 165–170°C in the tips is borrowed from that source (NGA091) and labelled as such.

INGREDIENT/METHOD MISMATCH, flagged: chilli powder and garlic both appear in the ingredient list but are not used in step 1; garlic appears in step 3; CHILLI POWDER APPEARS IN NEITHER STEP — it is in the list and absent from the method entirely.

DISAGREEMENT ON THE PROTEIN, and it resolves itself: this recipe uses ram, the Kitchen Butterfly version uses 2 kg of beef, and both are titled dambu nama. But that site's own dambu taxonomy settles it — beef is dambun nama or dambun saniya, ram is dambun rago. By the author's own naming system this is dambun rago, which is how it is titled here.

A NOTE ON THIS SOURCE TYPE, borne out across the research: Daily Trust proved strong on ethnography, named sellers and occasions, and almost never quantified. It is best used for headnote material rather than for measurements.
reheating: Eat as is, or refresh briefly in a dry pan.
healthBenefits: Very high in protein and very low in carbohydrate.
Ram is rich in iron, zinc and B12.
The frying fat is drained off.
Ginger and garlic both have documented anti-inflammatory activity.
culturalNote: Ram is the festival meat of northern Nigeria, and dambun rago is one of the things made from an animal slaughtered for Eid — a way of turning a large quantity of meat into something that keeps for weeks. The naming convention is precise about it: nama and saniya for beef, rago for ram, akuya for goat, rakumi for camel.
